newsitem.title: GERMANY: Nobel award turns poet into instant millionaire.
newsitem.headline: Nobel award turns poet into instant millionaire.

text.p: The award of the 1996 Nobel Literature Prize to Wislawa Szymborska will make the publicity-shy Polish poet a millionaire and reap a rich harvest for her publishers.
Extra sales generated by the award are set to propel her from relative obscurity to international literary stardom.
Dr Rainer Weiss, her German publisher, could barely contain his glee at the world's biggest book fair in Frankfurt when hearing the news from Stockholm of her $1.2 million award.
"Sales are bound to go up. They always do with a Nobel winner," said the editor-in-chief of Suhrkamp.

The spotlight is now firmly on the 73-year-old Szymborksa who confessed from a Polish mountain resort hotel for writers: "This is a difficult situation. I am normally a very private person and now I foresee some difficult moments."
When Seamus Heaney became Ireland's fourth Nobel literature prizewinner last year, his publisher reported 500,000 pounds worth of extra sales in the first three months afterwards.
"It was staggering. He was a very popular choice," said Joanna Mackle, publishing director of Faber and Faber. "Many more translations and rights were sold."

"He sells better than a winner of the Booker Prize (Britain's premier book award). That is pretty amazing for a poet. We publish 12 or 13 of his books and sales were at a much higher plateau after the Nobel."
Faber and Faber have seven Nobel prizewinners in their literary stable and Mackle said readers also flocked to buy the books of English author William Golding when he won in 1983.
U.S. publisher Roger Strauss boasts 20 Nobel prizewinners among his authors. They range from South African writer Nadine Gordimer to Caribbean poet Derek Walcott.
He agreed that an author's path to literary glory could be paved with gold after landing the world's most famous literature prize.

"When Isaac Singer won, there was an enormous jump in sales. He had a new novel just out and there was something new and fresh to offer," he told Reuters at the Frankfurt Book Fair, the world's leading marketplace for publishers.
"After Singer won, we sold him in 15 languages in just two days at the fair," Strauss said.
He reported the same reaction with Joseph Brodsky in 1987. "We immediately sold 20,000 copies straight off," he said.

Strauss said nothing among America's literary prizes could match the sales clout of the Nobel award. "It also means that with all future books you get to put the Nobel sticker on it. That increases sales for a long time."
